title: Coordinating Conjunctions (Ḥurūf al-ʿAṭf)
source: Original instructional lesson authored for this application (syllabus ref: Haywood & Nahmad Ch. 49; Ryding Ch. 18)
objectives: Distinguish the temporal/logical nuances of وَ, فَـ, ثُمَّ, أَوْ, أَمْ, and بَلْ.
Apply case and mood agreement across conjoined elements (al-maʿṭūf).
recallPrompt: From Chapter 1: Which conjunction drops hamzat al-waṣl in connected reading?

sections.heading: Precision in Classical Conjunctions
sections.body: Arabic coordinating conjunctions carry precise logical and temporal distinctions. Whereas English uses 'and' for almost everything, Arabic distinguishes simple simultaneity/association (وَ) from immediate consequence (فَـ) and sequence after a delay (ثُمَّ).

sections.label: Case & Mood Sharing (Al-ʿAṭf)
sections.summary: A conjoined noun or verb (al-maʿṭūf) always shares the grammatical case or mood of the preceding item (al-maʿṭūf ʿalayh).

sections.heading: Core Coordinating Conjunctions
rows: Succession after a pause or delay

sections.translation: I recited al-Fātiḥah and then (afterward) the sūrah.
sections.irab: الفَاتِحَةَ: مَفْعُولٌ بِهِ مَنْصُوبٌ | ثُمَّ: حَرْفُ عَطْفٍ | السُّورَةَ: مَعْطُوفٌ مَنْصُوبٌ
sections.notes: Because الفَاتِحَةَ is accusative, السُّورَةَ conjoined by ثُمَّ is also accusative.

sections.heading: أَوْ vs. أَمْ ('Or')
sections.body: أَوْ is used in statements and open questions; أَمْ is used after interrogative أَ to ask 'which of two?' (أَأَنْتَ كَتَبْتَ أَمْ هُوَ؟).
